title: The Tractatus and Its Formalization
content: The Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus opens: 'The world is everything that is the case.' What follows is an attempt to express the formal skeleton of that vision in Lean 4 — the ontology of objects, states of affairs, facts, and truth-functional propositions. We formalize the part that *can* be formalized, including a structural shadow of the saying/showing distinction (TLP 4.12-4.1212), and annotate where the philosophy exceeds the formalism.
mathContext: The Tractatus contains a nearly axiomatic ontology buried in its numbered propositions (1, 1.1, 2.01, 2.02, etc.). We extract and formalize the structural core: types for objects and states of affairs, a model-theoretic notion of world, an inductive grammar for propositions, and a recursive evaluation function. The result is a miniature model theory built from scratch, culminating in theorems about the limits of expression within the object language.

title: Mathlib Import
content: We import `Mathlib.Tactic` for proof automation (`simp`, `tauto`, etc.) and access to classical logic lemmas like `not_not` and `not_and_or`. The formalization is otherwise self-contained — no Mathlib theorems appear in the definitions, only in the proofs.

title: Objects: The Simple (TLP 2.02)
content:
TLP 2.02: 'The object is simple.' We model Tractarian objects as a `variable` type parameter — Lean knows nothing about its inhabitants except that the type exists. This captures Wittgenstein's insistence that objects have no analyzable internal structure.

**[Interpretive choice]** Using a bare type parameter captures *simplicity* (no structure) but not the Tractarian claim that an object's *form* determines which states of affairs it can enter (TLP 2.0141). A dependent-type encoding — where each object carries a type constraining its combinatorial possibilities — would better capture 2.0141 but at the cost of specifying structure Wittgenstein deliberately leaves open. We opt for the lighter encoding.
mathContext: In Lean, `variable (TractObject : Type)` introduces a universe-polymorphic type parameter. Any theorem or definition mentioning `TractObject` is implicitly universally quantified over all types — so our results hold regardless of what objects 'are.'

title: States of Affairs: Sachverhalte (TLP 2.01)
content:
TLP 2.01: 'An atomic fact is a combination of objects.' A state of affairs (*Sachverhalt*) is a possible way objects might combine. We model this as an abstract type parameter, just like objects.

**[Interpretive choice]** We do *not* encode states of affairs as sets of objects or as predicates over objects. The Tractatus arguably intends something more structural — the *way* objects hang together, not merely *which* objects are involved (the 'form' of TLP 2.032). By keeping Sachverhalt abstract, we preserve this openness. The cost is that we cannot express *within* the formalization how objects compose into states of affairs.
mathContext: The choice to keep `Sachverhalt` abstract rather than defining it as `Set TractObject -> Prop` or `List TractObject` is deliberate. An extensional encoding would commit us to saying that states of affairs with the same objects are identical — which conflicts with 'aRb' and 'bRa' being distinct states of affairs involving the same objects.

title: Worlds: The Totality of Facts (TLP 1, 2.04)
content:
TLP 1: 'The world is everything that is the case.' TLP 2.04: 'The totality of existing atomic facts is the world.' A world is a function `Sachverhalt -> Prop` — for each state of affairs, it says whether that state of affairs obtains.

This is the standard model-theoretic move: a 'world' or 'model' is a truth-value assignment to atomic propositions. What is distinctive about the Tractarian version is the ontological weight: for Wittgenstein, the world literally *is* the totality of facts, not something that *has* facts as properties.
mathContext: Defining `World` as `Sachverhalt -> Prop` means a world is a predicate on states of affairs. This is equivalent to a subset of `Sachverhalt` (via the correspondence `Set a = (a -> Prop)`). We use the predicate form because it integrates more naturally with Lean's type theory.

title: Propositions: The Inductive Grammar (TLP 4.21, 5)
content:
TLP 4.21: 'The simplest proposition, the elementary proposition, asserts the existence of an atomic fact.' TLP 5: 'The proposition is a truth-function of elementary propositions.'

We define propositions as an inductive type with three constructors: `elementary` (asserts a state of affairs), `neg` (negation), and `conj` (conjunction). Every proposition is a finite tree built from these constructors.

TLP 5.101 tells us that all truth-functions arise from successive applications of negation and conjunction. The other connectives — disjunction, implication, biconditional — are defined, not primitive.
mathContext: The `inductive` keyword in Lean defines a freely generated type. `Proposition S` is parametric in a type `S` of states of affairs. The three constructors give us a complete basis for propositional logic: {neg, and} is functionally complete (any Boolean function can be expressed using only negation and conjunction).

title: Derived Connectives (TLP 5.101)
content: TLP 5.101: 'The truth-functions of every number of elementary propositions can be written in a schema.' We define disjunction, implication, biconditional, and NAND from the primitives. The NAND gate (TLP 5.5) is historically significant: Wittgenstein recognized — independently of Sheffer (1913) — that a single binary operation suffices for all truth-functions.
mathContext: These definitions are not just convenient abbreviations. They demonstrate the Tractarian thesis that the expressive power of propositional logic reduces entirely to {neg, and}, and further to the single Sheffer stroke. The theorems below verify that these definitions produce the expected semantics.

title: Semantic Evaluation: Picture Theory (TLP 2.21, 4.06)
content:
TLP 2.21: 'The picture agrees with reality or not; it is right or wrong, true or false.' TLP 4.06: 'Propositions can be true or false only by being pictures of the reality.'

The `eval` function is the heart of the formalization. It recursively computes the truth value of a proposition relative to a world:
- An elementary proposition e(s) is true in world w iff the state of affairs s obtains in w
- neg p is true iff p is false
- p and q is true iff both p and q are true

This is Wittgenstein's picture theory reduced to its formal core: a proposition 'pictures' reality by having the same truth conditions.
mathContext: The function is defined by structural recursion on the `Proposition` inductive type. Lean automatically verifies that the recursion terminates because each recursive call is on a structurally smaller argument. The return type `Prop` means evaluation lives in Lean's universe of propositions — we are using Lean's logic to model Wittgenstein's.

title: Tautology and Contradiction (TLP 4.46, 6.1)
content:
TLP 4.46: 'Among the possible groups of truth-conditions there are two extreme cases.' TLP 6.1: 'The propositions of logic are tautologies.'

`IsTautology p` means p evaluates to true in *every* world. `IsContradiction p` means p evaluates to false in *every* world. These are the two extreme cases of TLP 4.46 — a tautology says nothing about which world is actual (it holds in all of them), while a contradiction rules out every possibility.
mathContext: Both definitions use universal quantification over `World S`. A tautology is forall w, eval(p, w); a contradiction is forall w, neg eval(p, w). The key philosophical point: for Wittgenstein, tautologies are not 'truths about the world' — they are limit cases that show the structure of logical space without saying anything about it.

title: Tautologies Are World-Invariant (TLP 6.1)
content: TLP 6.1: 'The propositions of logic are tautologies.' This theorem states that a proposition holds in every world if and only if it is a tautology. The proof is `rfl` — it holds by definition.
mathContext: The `rfl` tactic closes the goal because `IsTautology p` is definitionally equal to `forall w : World S, p.eval w`. In Lean's type theory, definitional equality means no proof is needed.

title: Contradictions Hold Nowhere (TLP 4.46)
content: If a proposition is a contradiction, it is false in every world. The proof is immediate from the definition.

title: Elementary Proposition Bivalence (TLP 4.023)
content:
TLP 4.023: 'The proposition determines reality to this extent, that one only needs to say "Yes" or "No" to it.' For any state of affairs s and world w, either s obtains in w or it does not.

The proof invokes `Classical.em` — the law of excluded middle. Wittgenstein assumes bivalence throughout the Tractatus, so classical logic is the appropriate foundation here.
mathContext: `Classical.em` provides P or neg P for any proposition P. The Tractatus is firmly classical.

title: Truth-Functional Compositionality (TLP 5)
content:
TLP 5: 'The proposition is a truth-function of elementary propositions.' This is the central theorem of the original formalization. It states: if two worlds agree on every elementary proposition, they agree on every compound proposition.

The proof proceeds by structural induction on the proposition. This is the formal content of 'truth-functionality': compound truth values are determined entirely by elementary truth values.
mathContext: The `induction p with` tactic performs structural induction on the `Proposition` type. The `Iff.not` and `Iff.and` lemmas lift biconditionals through negation and conjunction.

title: Logical Independence (TLP 2.061, 2.062)
content:
TLP 2.061: 'Atomic facts are independent of one another.' Given *any* truth-value assignment to states of affairs, there exists a world realizing it. The proof is beautifully trivial: in our encoding, a truth-value assignment literally *is* a `World S`.

**[Interpretive choice]** This triviality is both a strength and a limitation. Independence is *built into the encoding* rather than *proved from it*.
mathContext: The proof constructs the existential witness directly. `Iff.rfl` shows that the world's valuation is definitionally equal to the assignment — because they are the same function.

title: Double Negation (Classical Logic)
content: Double negation elimination: neg neg p iff p in every world. This uses classical logic, which the Tractatus assumes throughout.

title: De Morgan's Laws (TLP 5.101)
content: De Morgan's laws verify that our definitions of derived connectives produce the expected semantics. These confirm that the {neg, and} basis generates the full propositional calculus as Wittgenstein claims in TLP 5.101.
mathContext: The `simp` tactic with `not_and_or` and `not_not` rewrites the nested negations into the standard disjunctive form.

title: Excluded Middle as Tautology (TLP 4.46)
content: p or neg p is a tautology — it holds in every world. This is the paradigmatic example of TLP 6.1: a 'proposition of logic' that is true regardless of which states of affairs obtain.
mathContext: The proof first applies `simp` to reduce the disjunction (defined via double negation) to a standard form, then invokes `Classical.em`.

title: p and neg p Is a Contradiction
content: p and neg p holds in no world — the paradigmatic contradiction.

title: Implication and Biconditional Semantics
content: These theorems verify that the derived connectives have their standard semantics. The `tauto` tactic handles the classical propositional reasoning after `simp` normalizes the definitions.

title: Modus Ponens (Metalogical, TLP 4.121)
content:
If p implies q is true in a world and p is true in that world, then q is true in that world. This is a meta-theorem: it is proved in Lean (the metalanguage) *about* propositions in our object language.

This is precisely the kind of thing Wittgenstein says can be *shown* by the symbolism but not *said* within it (TLP 4.121: 'What can be shown cannot be said'). The formal system shows that modus ponens preserves truth — it does not contain a proposition asserting this fact. Our Lean theorem *says* what the Tractarian framework can only *show*.
mathContext: The proof rewrites the implication hypothesis using `impl_semantics`, then applies it to the premise.

title: NAND Functional Completeness (TLP 5.5)
content: TLP 5.5 anticipates the Sheffer stroke: all truth-functions can be derived from a single binary operation. We show that nand(p, p) gives negation and neg nand(p, q) gives conjunction. Since {neg, and} is functionally complete, NAND alone suffices.
mathContext: The first proof uses `tauto` after simplification. The second uses `not_not` to eliminate the double negation.

title: The Saying/Showing Distinction (TLP 4.12-4.1212)
content:
TLP 4.12: 'Propositions can represent the whole reality, but they cannot represent what they must have in common with reality in order to be able to represent it.' TLP 4.1212: 'What can be shown cannot be said.'

This section formalizes a structural analogue of the saying/showing distinction — not the philosophical thesis itself (which is arguably self-undermining), but a precise mathematical shadow of it. The key insight: metalinguistic properties like 'p is a tautology' are world-independent (they hold or fail regardless of which states of affairs obtain), but any proposition whose truth value is world-independent must be trivially a tautology or contradiction. Therefore the object language can only 'say' world-independent truths through its most degenerate members — propositions that carry no specific content.

**Overclaiming caveat**: We have formalized a *structural analogue* of Wittgenstein's thesis, not the thesis itself. Wittgenstein claims that logical form is *in principle* inexpressible in *any* language. What we prove is the narrower result that world-independent properties are inexpressible *non-trivially* in *this particular* propositional object language. The gap between these claims is philosophical, not mathematical.

**Historical note**: This result is a baby version of Tarski's undefinability theorem (1936), which shows that no sufficiently expressive language can define its own truth predicate. Wittgenstein's Tractatus (1921) anticipates the key insight by fifteen years: the semantic properties of a language cannot be stated within that language. Our formalization makes this anticipation precise for a propositional setting.
mathContext: The mathematical content reduces to a simple observation about world-constant functions: if q.eval w1 iff q.eval w2 for all w1, w2, then q is either true in all worlds (tautology) or false in all worlds (contradiction). This follows immediately from classical logic: pick any reference world, and excluded middle determines which case holds. The saying/showing theorems are corollaries.

title: World-Constant Propositions Are Trivial (TLP 4.46)
content:
A proposition whose truth value is the same in all worlds must be a tautology or a contradiction. This is the technical core of the saying/showing formalization.

The proof picks an arbitrary reference world (all states of affairs obtaining), checks whether q holds there using classical excluded middle, and then uses world-constancy to propagate the answer to all other worlds.

Philosophically, this captures TLP 4.46's claim that tautologies and contradictions are the *only* extreme cases: there is no middle ground for world-constant propositions. A proposition either says something about the world (and therefore varies across worlds) or it is trivial.
mathContext: The proof uses `by_cases hq : q.eval w0` which requires classical logic. In constructive logic, we could not decide whether q holds at the reference world, and the theorem would fail. This is appropriate: the Tractatus assumes bivalence throughout.

title: Saying/Showing Triviality (TLP 4.1212)
content:
TLP 4.1212: 'What can be shown cannot be said.' This theorem gives that claim precise mathematical content: any proposition q that expresses a world-independent property P (i.e., q.eval w iff P for all w) must be a tautology or contradiction.

The proof is a one-line application of world_constant_taut_or_contra: if q.eval w iff P for all w, and P does not depend on w, then q.eval w1 iff q.eval w2 for all w1, w2 (both are equivalent to the same P).

**Subtlety about formal vs. philosophical content**: In classical logic, every Prop P is either True or False (by excluded middle). So a matching tautology or contradiction always exists — P is always formally 'expressible' in the weak sense of q.eval w iff P. But this expression is trivial: the *same* tautology expresses *every* true metalinguistic fact, and the *same* contradiction expresses *every* false one. The proposition does not encode P specifically; it merely shares its truth value by logical coincidence.

This triviality — not inexpressibility — is the correct formal content of 'what can be shown cannot be said.' The original proposition_seven (which claimed outright inexpressibility) was mathematically incorrect; this triviality theorem replaces it with the right result.
mathContext: The key step is trans: from q.eval w1 iff P and P iff q.eval w2, we get q.eval w1 iff q.eval w2. This establishes world-constancy, and world_constant_taut_or_contra does the rest.

title: Contingent Propositions Vary Across Worlds
content:
The contrapositive of world-constancy: a proposition that is neither a tautology nor a contradiction must have different truth values in some pair of worlds. This is the semantic content of contingency — a proposition 'says' something about the world precisely because its truth depends on which world obtains.

Together with saying_showing_triviality, this gives a complete picture: propositions are partitioned into three classes. Tautologies (world-constant True), contradictions (world-constant False), and contingent propositions (world-varying). Only the third class carries non-trivial content about the world.

title: The Ladder (TLP 6.54)
content:
TLP 6.54: 'My propositions serve as elucidations in the following way: anyone who understands me eventually recognizes them as nonsensical, when he has used them — as steps — to climb beyond them. He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it.'

Everything above is the ladder. The view from the top — that logical form is shared between language and reality rather than represented by either — is precisely what Lean, or any formal system, shows through its structure rather than states as a theorem. The residue left over after formalization is the most Wittgensteinian part.

**[Interpretive choice]** The Tractatus is self-consciously paradoxical: it uses meaningful propositions to argue that certain things cannot be meaningfully said. Any formalization must pick a side — either the ladder is meaningful (in which case the self-undermining thesis fails) or it is not (in which case the formalization formalizes nothing). We take the first option: the formal skeleton is mathematically meaningful, and the philosophical claim about its limitations is carried by the annotations, not the code.

title: Proposition 7 (TLP 7)
content:
TLP 7: *Wovon man nicht sprechen kann, darueber muss man schweigen.* — 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.'

This theorem states: any attempt to express a world-independent truth P as a proposition q forces q into triviality — q must be a tautology or a contradiction. It is a direct corollary of saying_showing_triviality, serving as the capstone of the formalization.

**Correction of the original formulation**: The previous version of this theorem claimed the existence of an inexpressible Prop P (formally: there exists P such that no q satisfies forall w, q.eval w iff P). This statement is actually *false* in classical logic: for any P, excluded middle gives P or neg P, and in either case a tautology or contradiction serves as a witness. The corrected version captures the philosophical intent more precisely: world-independent truths are not *inexpressible* but *trivially* expressible — which is worse. A tautology 'says' every truth and no truth in particular. The silence of Proposition 7 is not that the object language *cannot* match P's truth value, but that in doing so it says nothing specific.

**Connection to Tarski (1936)**: Tarski's undefinability theorem shows that no sufficiently expressive language can define its own truth predicate. Our result is a propositional analogue: the object language cannot non-trivially express its own semantic properties (tautologousness, contradiction, etc.). Wittgenstein's Tractatus (1921) anticipates the key insight by fifteen years.
mathContext: The theorem is a direct application of saying_showing_triviality. The proof is: saying_showing_triviality q P h. No sorry remains — the theorem is fully machine-checked.
